messages.subject: How to calculate survey effort during CTDS?
parts:
Hello all, distance sampling newbie here.

Im doing some basic CTDS research for my PhD. Last year we did a test survey through 2 forest complexes to count density of 3 ungulate species (Roe, red deer and wildboar). I collected the data, put them in the tables in distance software, but analyse results seem to be completly unrealistic.

Well not gonna lie I am not mathematician, basically my math kinda ends when I am out of my fingers to count, but I figured out based on Howe et al. Duiker sheets that I need to input proper Survey Effort numbers, because 1 is definetly a wrong value there and making all the mess. The thing is I don't really understand how to calculate it properly. I found some info that "Survey effort at each camera trap location is the number of snapshot moments".

The problem is I can't simply understand what exactly that means for me. Do I count just the numbers of photos taken for each individual animal and sum them up? What about videos? And what if I just set higher number of photos than 3+30sec video that I was using here. What If some camera traps didn't observe any ungulate at all?

I guess these are probably pretty silly questions so sorry for that and hige thanks for help.

Robin

Welcome to the group.

Figuring out the effort associated with camera trapping is not simple, so don't be surprised if it baffles you.

I have broken down the calculation of effort for Howe et al.'s (2017) Maxwells duiker study that used motion sensor-triggered still photographs. The definition of a "snapshot moment" is key; it is the length of time for a camera and sensor to recycle to be ready to take another photo. For the equipment in Howe et al. (2017) that length of time was two seconds. The link below determines the number of those two-second "moments" for the cameras operating during the daily "peak activity period" of the animals over the ~3 month duration of the deployment.
https://erex.github.io/Oct-Quarto/announce/2023-01-15-cameraeffort/index.html

I can't give you a good answer to the definition of a "snapshot moment" when using other camera configurations. Perhaps others on the list may have experience with this.

An ancillary issue is field of view of your cameras/sensors. That also influences the definition of effort. The proportion of a circle "seen" by the cameras can be incorporated into the computation of effort, as done by Howe et al. (2017):

A camera trap (CT) is deployed at a point k that is independent of animal density for a period of time Tk and set to record images for as long as an animal is present to trigger it. We predetermine a finite set of snapshot moments within Tk, t units of time apart, at which an image of an animal could be obtained. Temporal effort at the point is then Tk/t. When images of animals are obtained, we estimate the horizontal radial distance ri between the midpoint of each animal and the camera, at each snapshot moment, for as long as it remains in view. If the camera covers an angle θ radians, then θ/2π describes the fraction of a circle covered by the camera, so we define overall sampling effort at point k as . We regard the data as a series of snapshots,
